facts.summary: Tennessee has no state overtime or daily-overtime law; overtime is governed entirely by the federal FLSA (time-and-a-half after 40 hours per week).
facts.sourceAgency: Tennessee Department of Labor & Workforce Development, Labor Standards Unit
facts.notes: Inferred from the fact that the Labor Standards Unit enforces only six labor laws (Child Labor Act, Wage Regulations Act, Prevailing Wage Act, Illegal Alien Act, Tennessee Lawful Employment Act, Non-Smoker Protection Act) — none of which set overtime rates. Verify no change if a state wage/hour statute is enacted.

facts.summary: Tennessee has no state minimum-wage statute, so the federal minimum wage of $7.25/hour applies.
facts.sourceAgency: Tennessee Department of Labor & Workforce Development, Labor Standards Unit
facts.notes: TN's Wage Regulations Act governs how/when wages are paid, not a minimum rate; no minimum-wage act is among the laws the Labor Standards Unit enforces. Federal $7.25 figure is the FLSA baseline, not a TN-published number. Re-verify against US DOL state table.

facts.summary: The Tennessee Human Rights Act bars employment discrimination based on race, creed, color, religion, sex, age (over 40), and national origin; the separate Tennessee Disability Act covers disability.
facts.citation: Tenn. Code Ann. § 4-21-101 et seq. (THRA); Tenn. Code Ann. § 8-50-103 et seq. (Tennessee Disability Act)
facts.sourceAgency: Tennessee Attorney General, Civil Rights Enforcement Division (CRED)
facts.notes: Largely mirrors the federal set; 'creed' is the main addition beyond Title VII/ADEA/ADA. Age protection is limited to individuals over 40, like the ADEA.

facts.value: Tennessee Disability Act prohibits disability discrimination
facts.summary: The Tennessee Disability Act separately prohibits employment discrimination against individuals based on disability, enforced alongside the THRA.
facts.sourceAgency: Tennessee Attorney General, Civil Rights Enforcement Division (CRED)
facts.notes: Official source confirms the statute prohibits disability discrimination but does not detail a reasonable-accommodation/interactive-process mandate; scope of accommodation duty should be verified against the statute text and case law before relying on it.

facts.value: 8 or more employees (1+ for retaliation claims)
facts.summary: The Tennessee Human Rights Act covers employers (private and public) with 8 or more employees within the state -- a lower threshold than federal Title VII/ADA's 15-employee floor -- while a retaliation claim can be brought against an employer with as few as 1 employee.
facts.notes: Confirmed directly against an official THRC presentation ('Employment: 8 or more employees/15 or more if filed with EEOC; At least 1 employee for retaliation claims'). No freely-accessible official full-text Tennessee Code portal was found this session to independently re-verify the exact codified definition text at § 4-21-102 (Tennessee's official code is behind a LexisNexis paywall) -- this entry relies on the THRC's own official summary rather than the raw statute text.

facts.value: Tennessee Public Protection Act (Whistleblower Law), Tenn. Code Ann. § 50-1-304
facts.summary: Tennessee's whistleblower statute protects employees from retaliatory discharge for refusing to participate in, or remain silent about, illegal activities.
facts.sourceAgency: Tennessee Department of Labor & Workforce Development
facts.notes: Tennessee also recognizes common-law retaliatory-discharge claims and statutory anti-retaliation protections tied to workers' comp claims (§ 50-6-101 et seq.), jury duty (§ 22-4-106), and military service (§ 8-33-101 et seq.).

facts.value: 180 days to file with CRED; 1 year to file a private THRA lawsuit
facts.summary: An employment discrimination complaint must be filed with the AG's Civil Rights Enforcement Division within 180 days of the last discriminatory act; a private THRA lawsuit must be filed within one year after the discriminatory practice ceases.
facts.sourceAgency: Tennessee Attorney General, Civil Rights Enforcement Division (CRED)
facts.notes: Per CRED FAQ, filing an administrative complaint does NOT toll the THRA's one-year statute of limitations for a private lawsuit. Civil-rights enforcement moved from the former Tennessee Human Rights Commission to the AG's CRED division.

facts.value: next regular payday or 21 days after separation, whichever is later
facts.summary: A departing employee (quit or discharged) must be paid all earned wages by the next regular payday or within 21 days of separation, whichever occurs last.
facts.sourceAgency: Tennessee Department of Labor & Workforce Development, Labor Standards Unit
facts.notes: This is a TN-specific timing rule with no direct federal equivalent.

facts.value: at least once per month (semi-monthly for many private employers)
facts.summary: Wages in private employment must be paid at least monthly, with additional scheduling requirements for employers using more frequent pay periods.
facts.sourceAgency: Tennessee Department of Labor & Workforce Development, Labor Standards Unit
facts.notes: State-specific wage-payment rule; federal FLSA sets no general pay-frequency requirement. Verify semi-monthly threshold details against statute text.

facts.value: 30-minute unpaid meal/rest period when scheduled 6 consecutive hours
facts.summary: Tennessee requires a 30-minute unpaid meal or rest period for employees scheduled to work six consecutive hours (with limited workplace exceptions).
facts.sourceAgency: Tennessee Department of Labor & Workforce Development, Labor Standards Unit
facts.notes: State addition beyond federal law, which does not mandate meal or rest breaks.

facts.value: 3 years (for causes of action arising on or after July 1, 2024)
facts.summary: Tennessee added an explicit 3-year statute of limitations for unpaid-wage claims - hours worked, overtime, minimum wage, salary, bonuses, commissions, or other compensation - effective for claims arising on or after July 1, 2024.
facts.notes: Enacted 2024 Pub. Ch. 747 (HB 2113/SB 2017), adding subdivision (4) to Tenn. Code Ann. § 28-3-105, which already sets a 3-year period for 'property tort actions [and] statutory liabilities.' Applies to causes of action accruing on/after 7/1/2024; wage claims accruing before that date may be governed by a different (e.g., general contract) limitations period - verify for pre-2024 claims.
